notes.claim: The rms value of an AC quantity is the DC that would produce the same heating in the same resistance.
For a sine wave the rms value is approximately 0.707 of the peak, which is the reciprocal of the square root of 2.
UK mains is 230 V rms, so its peak is about 325 V (230 times root 2), according to one school revision site; the nominal 230 V itself is set by ESQCR.
For i2: an analogue meter's needle follows the average of the AC, and its rms calibration assumes a sine wave (screens 9, 10 and 12, the explain and practice).
For i2: appliances and devices are quoted with rms values rather than peak values (the explain and the practice's first bullet).
For i2: most ships run a 440 V system, so as an example its peak is 440 x root 2 = 622 V (computed; SECONDARY; screen 8's Why? and the explain).

sources.quote: Misconception: Peak voltage is the same as mains voltage. Correction: UK mains voltage is 230 V RMS, so the peak voltage is about 325 V (230 × √2).

sources.quote: UK mains electricity operates at a nominal voltage of 230V, and can operate within limits of 253V and 216V set by the Electricity Safety, Quality and Continuity Regulations (ESQCR)

sources.quote: analog meters must be specifically calibrated (or mis-calibrated, depending on how you look at it) to indicate voltage or current in RMS units. The accuracy of this calibration depends on an assumed waveshape, usually a sine wave.

sources.title: maritime electrical installations - notes on design ...
sources.quote: The majority of ships have a 3 phase, 3 wire, 440V insulated neutral system. This means that the neutral point of star connected generators is not earthed to the ship's hull. For Continental European vessels, a 380V, 3 phase system is common.
